blurb: Is the Bermuda Triangle real? Meatball investigates its four most famous disappearances, Star Tiger (1948), the Marine Sulphur Queen (1963), Flight 19 (1945) and the USS Cyclops (1918), and checks each against the official records. Three are explained. One is still a real mystery. Sources are in the description.

sources: NOAA Ocean Service, 'What is the Bermuda Triangle?': no evidence that mysterious disappearances occur with greater frequency there than in any other large, well-traveled area of ocean; the US Board on Geographic Names does not recognize the name — https://oceanservice.noaa.gov/facts/bermudatri.html

Flight 19 (5 Dec 1945): five TBM Avengers, 14 airmen, NAS Fort Lauderdale training flight; leader Lt Charles Taylor reported compass failure and believed he was over the Keys; PBM Mariner (13 crew) lost on the search, SS Gaines Mills reported flames; Navy Board of Investigation — US Naval History and Heritage Command, 'The Loss of Flight 19' https://www.history.navy.mil/research/library/online-reading-room/title-list-alphabetically/l/loss-of-flight-19.html ; Wikipedia, Flight 19

Star Tiger (30 Jan 1948): BSAA Avro Tudor IV, Azores to Bermuda, 31 aboard (25 passengers, 6 crew), no distress call or wreckage; Ministry of Civil Aviation report: 'no more baffling problem has ever been presented for investigation'; Star Ariel lost 17 Jan 1949 (Bermuda to Jamaica); Tudor IVs withdrawn from passenger service — Wikipedia, BSAA Star Tiger disappearance / BSAA Star Ariel disappearance

SS Marine Sulphur Queen (Feb 1963): converted T2 tanker, ~15,000 long tons of molten sulfur, 39 crew, lost off the Florida Keys; debris incl. life jackets and a foghorn recovered; Coast Guard Marine Board found structural weakness and fire risk from the conversion — Wikipedia, SS Marine Sulphur Queen (cites the USCG Marine Board report)

USS Cyclops (AC-4), March 1918: left Barbados for Baltimore with 306 aboard and manganese ore, one engine damaged, never found; the largest single loss of life in US Navy history not involving combat; sister ships Proteus and Nereus lost in the North Atlantic in Nov/Dec 1941 — US Naval History and Heritage Command, 'USS Cyclops' https://www.history.navy.mil/research/library/online-reading-room/title-list-alphabetically/u/uss-cyclops.html ; Wikipedia, USS Cyclops (AC-4)

Name: Vincent Gaddis, 'The Deadly Bermuda Triangle', Argosy, Feb 1964; Charles Berlitz, The Bermuda Triangle (1974); Larry Kusche, The Bermuda Triangle Mystery: Solved (1975) found many stories exaggerated or wrong; Lloyd's of London and the US Coast Guard do not treat the area as unusually dangerous — Wikipedia, Bermuda Triangle

ask.q:
WHICH ONE IS STILL
A MYSTERY?

beats.say: I'm Meatball, by the way. I investigate weird stuff, and I tell you what's actually true. Subscribe. New case every Tuesday and Saturday.
Number four. January nineteen forty-eight. An airliner called Star Tiger is flying from the Azores to Bermuda. Thirty-one people on board.

shots.photo: Avro Tudor airliner of British South American Airways

beats.say: Near the end, the radio operator asks for a position check. Everything sounds normal. Then, nothing. No mayday. No wreck. No bodies.
The official inquiry wrote, and I'm quoting, that no more baffling problem had ever been presented to them. That sentence sold a lot of books.

shots.photo: Avro Tudor airliner of British South American Airways

beats.say: Ships and planes searched for five days. They covered thousands of square miles of ocean. They found nothing at all.
Here's the thing. The Tudor was a troubled plane. It flew low into strong headwinds to save fuel, and it had almost no spare fuel to fight them with.

shots.photo: Avro Tudor airliner of British South American Airways

beats.say: A year later, its sister plane, Star Ariel, vanished too. Not even in the Triangle's usual corner. The model was soon pulled from passenger service.

shots.photo: Avro Tudor airliner of British South American Airways

beats.say: If I flew that low, over that much water, on that little fuel, I'd also go quiet. Out of fear.
Verdict: a lost plane, not a cursed sea. Busted. And that's the easy one. Number three left wreckage behind, and it's worse.
Number three. February nineteen sixty-three. A tanker called the Marine Sulphur Queen leaves Texas carrying fifteen thousand tons of molten sulfur.

shots.photo: Debris from the SS Marine Sulphur Queen (US Coast Guard)

beats.say: Liquid sulfur. Kept hot. Inside a ship. That's already the scariest sentence in this video, and I live in a frying pan.
Thirty-nine crew. Its last radio message is routine. Then it's gone, off the Florida Keys, inside the Triangle.
Nine days later, the Coast Guard started searching. Nine days. Because nobody noticed it was late.

shots.obs: wm:Infrared imagery of Gulf Stream off the Virginia Capes (2268-445).jpg

beats.say: But this time the sea gave something back. Searchers found debris, life jackets and a foghorn.

shots.photo: Debris from the SS Marine Sulphur Queen (US Coast Guard)

beats.say: Here's the twist. The Coast Guard investigated, and the ship was the problem. It was an old tanker, rebuilt for hot cargo, with weak spots in its hull and reports of fires.

shots.photo: Debris from the SS Marine Sulphur Queen (US Coast Guard)

shots.obs: wm:Infrared imagery of Gulf Stream off the Virginia Capes (2268-445).jpg

beats.say: The board's conclusion: it should never have been allowed to sail like that. A sad, ordinary disaster.
So, no curse. But number two is the one that made the Triangle famous. Five bombers, one radio, and a rescue plane that also vanished.
If you're enjoying the investigation, hit like. It helps me find more cases.
Number two. December fifth, nineteen forty-five. Five Navy torpedo bombers take off from Fort Lauderdale on a training flight. Flight Nineteen.
The flight leader radios that his compasses are out. He thinks he's over the Florida Keys. He's probably not.
Other pilots hear him on the radio. They tell him to fly west, toward land. The flight turns, and turns again, as the weather gets worse and the light goes.
Then, the radio goes silent. Fourteen airmen. Gone.
Wait, it gets worse. A rescue flying boat goes out to search. Thirteen crew. It disappears too.

shots.obs: wm:Martin PBM-5 Mariner in flight, circa in 1945 (SDASM 00006374).jpg

beats.say: That's the part that sounds supernatural. Here's the catch. Those flying boats were nicknamed flying gas tanks, because fuel vapor leaked inside. That night a ship saw flames over the sea.

shots.obs: wm:Martin PBM-5 Mariner in flight, circa in 1945 (SDASM 00006374).jpg

beats.say: And the bombers? Lost, low on fuel, over a dark winter sea. They most likely ditched and sank. The Navy never found them. Neither did anyone else.
So I went to look for them myself. In a bathtub. It's a start.
Verdict: tragic, but explained. Lost bombers out of fuel, and a rescue plane that likely exploded. Busted.
Three down, and none of them were the sea. But number one is different. I promised you the one nobody can explain. Here it is.

shots.photo: USS Cyclops in the Hudson River, 1911 (US Navy)

beats.say: Number one. March nineteen eighteen. The USS Cyclops, one of the biggest ships in the US Navy, leaves Barbados for Baltimore.

shots.photo: USS Cyclops in the Hudson River, 1911 (US Navy)

shots.obs: wm:Plans for the USS Cyclops (AC-4) - NARA - 88697598.jpg

beats.say: Three hundred and six people on board. Its hold is packed with manganese ore. Heavy. Very heavy. More than it was meant to carry.

shots.obs: wm:Plans for the USS Cyclops (AC-4) - NARA - 88697598.jpg

shots.photo: USS Cyclops in the Hudson River, 1911 (US Navy)

beats.say: And one of its two engines is damaged. It's limping. It never sends a distress call. It never arrives.

shots.photo: USS Cyclops in the Hudson River, 1911 (US Navy)

beats.say: No wreck. No lifeboat. No oil slick. To this day, it's the largest loss of life in US Navy history that didn't happen in combat.
Here's the creepy part. In nineteen forty-one, two of its sister ships, built to the same design, also vanished in the Atlantic. Same design. Same silence.

shots.obs: wm:Plans for the USS Cyclops (AC-4) - NARA - 88697598.jpg

beats.say: There are wilder theories. A German submarine. A mutiny. A giant squid. The war records show no German submarine claimed it, and squid don't eat Navy ships.

shots.obs: wm:Plans for the USS Cyclops (AC-4) - NARA - 88697598.jpg

beats.say: That's actually the best clue. Overloaded, damaged, top-heavy ships in a storm can break up or roll over in minutes. Too fast to radio for help.
I also roll over in minutes. I'm round. It's a design flaw.
But nobody has ever found it, so nobody can prove it. Verdict: still a real mystery. Unsolved. And no, that doesn't mean a curse.

shots.photo: USS Cyclops in the Hudson River, 1911 (US Navy)

beats.say: So, is the Bermuda Triangle real? As a place, sure. It's one of the busiest stretches of ocean on Earth, with the Gulf Stream and sudden storms.

shots.obs: wm:Infrared imagery of Gulf Stream off the Virginia Capes (2268-445).jpg

beats.say: But the US government's ocean agency says there's no evidence ships vanish there more often than in any other busy patch of sea. Insurers don't charge extra to cross it.
A writer named it in nineteen sixty-four, books made it famous, and some of the stories they told turned out to be wrong.

shots.obs: wm:The missing Training Ship, HMS 'Atlanta' - The Graphic 1880.jpg

beats.say: So, were you right? Which one is still a mystery? Tell me in the comments.
